fetched_contents.title: How do I use the abortion pill?
fetched_contents.text: Planned Parenthood home Here's what you need to know about how to take abortion pills. How do I take abortion pills? At Planned Parenthood, before you take the abortion pills, you’ll meet with a nurse or doctor, either in person at the health center, or by video or phone, to go over how to take the pills. Your doctor or nurse will give you detailed directions about when and how to take the pills. Your doctor or nurse will give you 2 different medicines to end your pregnancy: mifepristone and misoprostol. Once you get your medicine, you can have your abortion at home or in another comfortable place that you choose. First, you’ll take a pill called mifepristone (200 milligrams (mg)). Pregnancy needs a hormone called progesterone to grow normally. Mifepristone blocks your body’s own progesterone, which stops the pregnancy from growing. Then you’ll take the second medicine, misoprostol, either right away or up to 48 hours later. 30 minutes before you take misoprostol: * Take pain medicine to help with cramps. Ibuprofen (Advil or Motrin) works the best, but you can take a different pain medicine like acetaminophen (Tylenol) if you need to. But don’t take aspirin because it can make you bleed more. * Take medicine for nausea if you have it. How do I take the second medicine? There are a few different ways to take misoprostol. You can put the pills in your vagina (vaginal), under your tongue (sublingual), or in your mouth between your cheeks and gums (buccal). They’ll slowly break down, and your body will absorb the medicine through the skin in your vagina or mouth. Don’t just swallow the pills — this will make them not work as well, and will probably make you feel very nauseous. Your doctor or nurse will talk you through the best way for you to take the pills. Here are the steps for each method: Buccal Take 24-48 hours after you take mifepristone. * Tuck 2 pills between your cheek and your gum on the side of your mouth. Do the same thing with 2 more pills on the other side of your mouth (800 micrograms (µg) of misoprostol total). * Leave them there for 30 minutes. * If there are still pieces of the pills left after 30 minutes, swallow them with water. Sublingual Take 24-48 hours after you take mifepristone. * Put 4 misoprostol pills (800 micrograms (µg) total) under your tongue. * Leave them there for 30 minutes. * If there are still pieces of the pills left after 30 minutes, swallow them with water. Vaginal Insert 0-48 hours after you take mifepristone. * Wash your hands. * Put 4 pills (800 micrograms (µg) total) deep into your vagina, as far as they’ll go. Put in 1 pill at a time. * Lay down for 30 minutes so they don’t fall out. * Pieces of the pills may fall out of your vagina later. If it’s been more than 30 minutes since you put that dose of pills in your vagina, your body should have absorbed enough of the medicine so you don’t need to put them back in. Some people will need a second dose of misoprostol. If your nurse or doctor tells you to take a second dose, you’ll take 4 more misoprostol pills (800 micrograms (µg) total) 4 hours later. Misoprostol causes cramping and bleeding, which empties your uterus. If you don’t have any bleeding within 24 hours after taking the second medicine, call your nurse or doctor. How do I know if the abortion pill worked? Abortion pills work really well. Exactly how well depends on how far along you are in your pregnancy when you take the medicine, and how many doses of misoprostol you take. Abortion pills usually work — but if they don’t, you can take more medicine or have an in-clinic abortion to complete the abortion. If you get your abortion pills from a health care provider like Planned Parenthood, they may give you a special, extra-sensitive pregnancy test to use after your abortion. You may also be able to get an ultrasound or blood test to confirm that the abortion worked. Your nurse or doctor will also talk you through everything you need to know. Regular pregnancy tests that you get at the store and some health centers may give you a false positive result for up to 5 weeks after your abortion — that’s because it takes a while for the pregnancy hormones to leave your body, and the test can pick those up, but it doesn’t mean you’re pregnant. However, it IS possible to get pregnant very soon after an abortion — even if pregnancy tests are coming up positive or your period hasn’t started yet. So if you’ve had sex without using birth control since having an abortion, a positive pregnancy test could mean that you’re pregnant again. If you’re not on hormonal birth control, you should have a period within 8 weeks after your abortion. If you’re not using hormonal birth control and you don’t get your period 8 weeks after your abortion, call your doctor or a Planned Parenthood health center.

fetched_contents.text: Questions and Answers on Mifepristone for Medical Termination of Pregnancy Through Ten Weeks Gestation On this page: * General Information * The Mifepristone REMS Program * Additional Information * The January 2023 REMS Modification * Litigation and Other Legal Issues General Information 1. What is mifepristone and how does it work? Mifepristone is a drug that blocks a hormone called progesterone that is needed for a pregnancy to continue. Mifepristone, when used together with another medicine called misoprostol, is used to end an intrauterine pregnancy through ten weeks gestation (70 days or less since the first day of the last menstrual period). The approved mifepristone dosing regimen is: * On day one: 200 mg of mifepristone taken by mouth * 24 to 48 hours after taking mifepristone: 800 mcg of misoprostol taken buccally (in the cheek pouch), at a location appropriate for the patient * About seven to fourteen days after taking mifepristone: follow-up with the health care provider 2. When did the FDA approve mifepristone for medical termination of pregnancy? The FDA first approved Mifeprex (mifepristone) in September 2000 for medical termination of pregnancy through seven weeks gestation, and this was extended to ten weeks gestation in 2016. FDA approved a generic version of Mifeprex, Mifepristone Tablets, 200 mg, in April 2019. The agency’s approval of this generic reflects the FDA’s determination that Mifepristone Tablets, 200 mg, is therapeutically equivalent to Mifeprex and can be safely substituted for Mifeprex. Like Mifeprex, the approved generic product is indicated for the medical termination of an intrauterine pregnancy through 70 days gestation. The labeling for the approved generic version of Mifeprex is consistent with the labeling for Mifeprex. 3. Who should not take mifepristone, in a regimen with misoprostol, for medical termination of pregnancy? An individual should not take mifepristone, in a regimen with misoprostol, for medical termination of pregnancy if it has been more than 70 days since the first day of their last menstrual period, or if they: * have an ectopic pregnancy (a pregnancy outside of the uterus) * have problems with the adrenal glands (the glands near the kidneys) * are currently being treated with long-term corticosteroid therapy * have had an allergic reaction to mifepristone, misoprostol or similar drugs * have bleeding problems or are taking anticoagulant (blood thinning) drug products * have inherited porphyria (a rare disorder that can affect the liver and other organs) * have an intrauterine device (IUD) in place (it must be removed before taking mifepristone) 4. Is it safe to use mifepristone? Yes. Mifepristone is safe when used as indicated and directed and consistent with the Mifepristone Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) Program. The FDA approved Mifeprex more than 20 years ago based on a thorough and comprehensive review of the scientific evidence presented and determined that it was safe and effective for its indicated use. As of 2016, it is approved for use for medical termination of pregnancy up to 70 days of gestation. The FDA’s periodic reviews of the postmarketing data for Mifeprex and its approved generic have not identified any new safety concerns with the use of mifepristone for medical termination of pregnancy through 70 days gestation. As with all drugs, the FDA continues to closely monitor the postmarketing safety data on mifepristone for the medical termination of pregnancy. 5. What are the possible side effects of using mifepristone for medical termination of pregnancy through ten weeks gestation? The possible side effects are described in the labeling and in the Medication Guide for mifepristone. 6. What serious adverse events have been reported after the use of mifepristone for medical termination of pregnancy through ten weeks gestation? As with all approved drugs, when the FDA receives new information regarding adverse events, the agency reviews the new information and, as appropriate, takes necessary action. This could include, for example, providing updates to health care providers and their patients so that they have information on how to use a drug safely. It is common for the FDA to receive reports of serious adverse events for prescription drugs after they are approved. Many drugs are associated with serious adverse events that are known at the time of approval and considered when the FDA makes its approval decision. The FDA continuously reviews reports of adverse events to, among other things, determine whether they are known risks or whether they are signals of emerging safety concerns. The FDA has received reports of serious adverse events in patients who took mifepristone. As of December 31, 2024, there were 36 reports of deaths in patients associated with mifepristone since the product was approved in September 2000, including two cases of ectopic pregnancy (a pregnancy located outside the womb, such as in the fallopian tubes) resulting in death, and several fatal cases of severe systemic infection (also called sepsis). The adverse events cannot with certainty be causally attributed to mifepristone because of concurrent use of other drugs, other medical or surgical treatments, co-existing medical conditions, and information gaps about patient health status and clinical management of the patient. A summary report of adverse events that reflects data through December 31, 2024, is here. The FDA has reviewed this information and did not identify any new safety signals. The FDA intends to update this summary report as appropriate. 7. Medication abortion has been available in the United States since 2000, when the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the use of mifepristone for abortion in a two-drug regimen with misoprostol. Mifepristone was first approved for use through seven weeks’ gestational duration and is currently approved through 10 weeks. It is also used safely off-label later in pregnancy. Unlike procedural abortion, medication abortion does not have to take place in a clinical setting—the pills can be taken in one’s own home. Decades of studies have shown that medication abortion is safe and effective. In 2023, medication abortion accounted for 63% of all clinician-provided abortions in states without total bans, up from 53% in 2020 and 39% in 2017. In the wake of Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, the US Supreme Court decision in June 2022 that overturned the federal constitutional right to abortion, states across the country instituted total or early gestational duration abortion bans that prohibit both procedural and medication abortion. In January 2023, the FDA lifted restrictions that prevented patients from obtaining medication abortion pills at a retail pharmacy. Pharmacies must complete a certification form from the manufacturer to dispense the pills. Individuals cannot obtain the medication at a pharmacy in states that have a total abortion ban. Many of the states that allow abortion have imposed unnecessary restrictions on medication abortion that increase barriers to care. For example, half of all states limit its provision solely to physicians. This policy contradicts findings from the World Health Organization and other health and medical organizations that advanced practice clinicians, such as physician assistants and advanced practice registered nurses, can safely provide medication abortion. Some states explicitly prohibit the use of telemedicine to provide medication abortion, despite clinical evidence that this practice is appropriate and safe. Other ways to prevent telemedicine provision in practice include requiring an in-person exam before the medications are provided, requiring a provider and patient to be in the same room when the medications are dispensed, and requiring that a provider observe a patient taking the first dose. A few states prohibit a provider from mailing abortion pills to a patient. In some states, providers are required to give patients medically inaccurate information on the possibility of “reversing” a medication abortion after starting the regimen. Patients may be required to make an in-person visit after taking the course of medication abortion, necessitating another trip to the provider. Several states specify a cut-off for use of medication abortion that is earlier than the FDA’s approved timeframe.

Risks and limitations of doing it at home without professional oversight

Home use of medication abortion carries several important risks and limitations, even though the regimen itself may be familiar in general terms. First, the evidence shows that complications and incomplete abortion are possible, and follow-up is essential. Planned Parenthood notes that some people will need follow-up treatment to complete the abortion, and that follow-up appointments are important to make sure the abortion is complete and the person is feeling well [N4-R2]. The Cleveland Clinic similarly states that follow-up is recommended within 2 to 5 weeks, and that follow-up appointments may ask the patient to come in for further care [N4-R1]. This indicates that home use is not a substitute for ongoing oversight.

A second major limitation is that the safety and effectiveness of the regimen depend on precise timing, dosage, and method of administration. The FDA’s Q&A explains that mifepristone and misoprostol are approved together for intrauterine pregnancy through ten weeks gestation, with specific dosing: 200 mg mifepristone orally on day one, then 800 mcg misoprostol buccally 24 to 48 hours later, and follow-up with a healthcare provider about 7 to 14 days after mifepristone [N2-F2]. The Planned Parenthood source adds that misoprostol causes cramping and bleeding, which empties the uterus, and that if bleeding does not occur within 24 hours after the second medicine, the patient should call a nurse or doctor [N1-F1]. This means that self-guided use can miss critical safety checks and may lead to delayed recognition of problems.

A third limitation is that self-directed use can mask serious complications or delay emergency care. The FDA’s Q&A emphasizes that serious adverse events can occur, including deaths from ectopic pregnancy or sepsis, and that healthcare providers should watch for signs and symptoms in patients who have taken mifepristone [N2-F2]. The Better Health Channel states that around 2% to 5% of people who have a medication abortion will need some follow-up treatment to complete the abortion [N4-R2]. That risk is not trivial and is why follow-up is explicitly recommended. The Royal Women’s Hospital similarly stresses that follow-up is important to make sure the abortion is complete and the person is feeling well [N4-R3]. Without that oversight, complications such as incomplete abortion, heavy bleeding, infection, or ectopic pregnancy may go unrecognized until they become urgent.

A fourth limitation is that legal and provider-guided requirements may prevent full self-direction. The Guttmacher Institute explains that many states impose restrictions on medication abortion, such as requiring in-person visits after the regimen, limiting provision to physicians only, or prohibiting mailing abortion pills [N3-F3]. These restrictions exist even when the FDA-approved regimen is medically appropriate, which shows that self-directed care may not be legally available in many jurisdictions. The same source also notes that states may require medically inaccurate information about “reversing” medication abortion, which can confuse patients and undermine informed choice [N3-F3]. This means that even if a person wants to do it at home, they may face legal barriers that require provider involvement.

Finally, self-guided use is limited by the inability to confirm accurate gestational age and pregnancy status. The evidence in this wave does not provide a detailed home-based pregnancy-dating method, but it does show that accurate dating is important for eligibility and safety. The FDA’s Q&A explicitly ties mifepristone use to gestational duration and states that the regimen is approved for pregnancy through ten weeks gestation [N2-F2]. Because gestational age determines eligibility, the lack of provider confirmation can lead to using the regimen too early or too late, with different safety profiles and outcomes. In short, the risks of home use are not just logistical: they include incomplete abortion, complications, delayed care, legal barriers, and the inability to verify that the regimen is appropriate for the patient’s actual pregnancy.

Overall, the evidence supports a clear conclusion: self-guided medication abortion is not a safe or reliable substitute for provider-guided care. The regimen is technically straightforward in some sources, but its safety depends on timing, correct administration, follow-up, and accurate pregnancy confirmation [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-R2]. Without professional oversight, the risks of complications and incomplete abortion increase, and the patient may miss critical signs that require immediate medical attention [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-R3].

What a patient should know before attempting a home medication abortion

Before attempting a home medication abortion, a patient should understand four key things: pregnancy duration and gestational age affect eligibility, the exact medications and how they should be taken, what screening or confirmation is needed before starting, and the contraindications and red flags that require stopping.

First, pregnancy duration and gestational age are central to eligibility. The FDA states that mifepristone, when used together with misoprostol, is approved for intrauterine pregnancy through ten weeks gestation (70 days or less since the first day of the last menstrual period) [N2-F2]. The Guttmacher Institute notes that several studies have reported medical abortion up to 9 weeks gestation through telemedicine services as safe and generally well tolerated, but it also emphasizes that legal restrictions may require earlier provider involvement in some states [N3-F3]. The ACOG practice bulletin similarly notes that most patients at 70 days of gestation or less who desire abortion are eligible for a medication abortion, but that there are medical conditions for which medication abortion may not be appropriate [N3-R2]. This means that gestational age is not just a numerical limit; it determines whether the regimen is medically appropriate and whether the patient meets the FDA-approved window.

Second, the medications used are mifepristone and misoprostol, and they should be taken in a specific sequence and method. The FDA-approved regimen is 200 mg mifepristone orally on day one, then 800 mcg misoprostol buccally 24 to 48 hours later, with follow-up with a healthcare provider about 7 to 14 days after mifepristone [N2-F2]. Planned Parenthood describes the home steps in more detail: first take mifepristone, then misoprostol 24 to 48 hours later, and for misoprostol, the preferred methods are buccal, sublingual, or vaginal, with specific instructions on how to place the pills and leave them for 30 minutes [N1-F1]. The same source stresses that the pills should not be swallowed, because that may make them less effective and more likely to cause nausea [N1-F1]. This shows that the regimen is not simply “take two pills” but requires precise timing and administration.

Third, screening or confirmation is needed before starting. The FDA explicitly states that mifepristone should not be used if the pregnancy is more than 70 days since the first day of the last menstrual period, and it lists several contraindications including ectopic pregnancy, adrenal problems, long-term corticosteroid use, bleeding problems, anticoagulant use, inherited porphyria, and an IUD in place [N2-F2]. The Cleveland Clinic adds that medical abortion is contraindicated in patients who are too far along, allergic to the medications, have ectopic pregnancy, or use certain other medications [N4-R4]. The Guttmacher Institute also notes that many states require in-person visits after starting the regimen and that some states prohibit mailing abortion pills [N3-F3]. In other words, provider confirmation is not optional; it is a necessary part of the process to establish eligibility and identify any red flags.

Fourth, contraindications and red flags that require stopping are important. The FDA’s Q&A states that mifepristone is contraindicated in patients with confirmed or suspected ectopic pregnancy, and that it should not be used if the pregnancy is more than 70 days since the first day of the last menstrual period [N2-F2]. The Cleveland Clinic similarly lists ectopic pregnancy and allergy to the medications as contraindications [N4-R4]. The IPAS source adds that mifepristone and misoprostol do not treat ectopic pregnancy and may delay diagnosis and treatment of this life-threatening condition [N2-R3]. The evidence also shows that serious adverse events can occur, including deaths from ectopic pregnancy or sepsis, and that healthcare providers should watch for signs and symptoms in patients who have taken mifepristone [N2-F2]. This means that the patient should not proceed if they have any of these red flags, and should instead seek provider assessment immediately.

In summary, a patient should know that home medication abortion is only appropriate if pregnancy duration and gestational age are within the approved window, that mifepristone and misoprostol must be taken in a specific sequence and method, that screening and provider confirmation are required before starting, and that several contraindications and red flags require stopping rather than proceeding [N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-R4][N1-F1]. These points are not optional details; they are central to safety and eligibility.

How to confirm pregnancy and dating in practice

To confirm pregnancy and dating in practice, a patient should use a combination of pregnancy tests and provider-based evaluation, because pregnancy confirmation alone is not sufficient to determine gestational age or safety. The evidence in this wave does not provide a single, universally definitive home pregnancy-dating method, but it does support a standard approach: pregnancy tests plus provider-based dating.

First, pregnancy can be confirmed with a pregnancy test. The evidence shows that medication abortion is discussed in the context of pregnancy confirmation, which implies that a positive pregnancy test is a prerequisite to starting the regimen [N2-F2][N3-R3]. Planned Parenthood also notes that after an abortion, regular pregnancy tests may give false positives for up to 5 weeks, and that this is because pregnancy hormones take time to leave the body [N1-F1]. This means that a home pregnancy test can confirm pregnancy, but it is not a reliable indicator of gestational age or whether the regimen is appropriate.

Second, gestational age is calculated using the last menstrual period (LMP) or ultrasound, and this is important for eligibility and safety. The FDA’s Q&A explicitly ties mifepristone use to gestational duration, stating that the regimen is approved for pregnancy through ten weeks gestation [N2-F2]. The ACOG methods paper states that ultrasound measurement of the embryo or fetus in the first trimester is the most accurate method to establish or confirm gestational age, especially up to and including 13 weeks and 6/7 days of gestation [N6-R5]. The due date calculators and pregnancy-dating tools cited in the search results also show that gestational age and due date are calculated from LMP or ultrasound dates [N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. In other words, gestational age is not merely a number; it is a clinical estimate that determines whether the regimen is medically appropriate.

Third, accurate dating is important because it affects eligibility and safety. The FDA’s approval is tied to gestational age, and the ACOG guidance emphasizes that provider-based dating is essential for determining whether a medication abortion is appropriate [N2-F2][N6-R5]. The Guttmacher Institute also notes that many states impose restrictions on medication abortion that may require earlier provider involvement, which suggests that accurate dating is a practical barrier to self-directed care [N3-F3]. The evidence further supports the idea that dating is important because the regimen’s safety and effectiveness depend on how far along the pregnancy is when the pills are started [N1-F1][N2-F2]. A late or uncertain date may mean that the patient is outside the FDA-approved window, which changes the risk profile.

Fourth, if dating is uncertain or late, the patient should not proceed without provider confirmation. The FDA explicitly states that mifepristone should not be used if the pregnancy is more than 70 days since the first day of the last menstrual period [N2-F2]. The Cleveland Clinic and other sources also list ectopic pregnancy as a contraindication and emphasize that medical abortion is not appropriate if the pregnancy is too far along [N4-R4]. The evidence does not provide a specific home method for resolving uncertain dating, but it does show that provider confirmation is required before starting the regimen [N2-F2][N3-F3]. In other words, when dating is uncertain, the safest course is to seek provider assessment rather than self-diagnose.

Overall, the evidence supports a practical workflow: pregnancy is first confirmed with a test, gestational age is determined by LMP or ultrasound, and accurate dating is essential because it determines eligibility and safety [N2-F2][N6-R5][N6-R1]. If dating is uncertain or late, provider confirmation is needed before proceeding, because the regimen is only approved within a specific gestational window and because inaccurate dating can lead to inappropriate use [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The search results also highlight that some states require in-person visits after starting the regimen, reinforcing the importance of provider oversight in dating and eligibility decisions [N3-F3].

## 1) What the patient should know before attempting a home medication abortion

Before proceeding, a patient should understand four key things: pregnancy duration and gestational age affect eligibility, the exact medications and how they should be taken, what screening or confirmation is needed before starting, and the contraindications and red flags that require stopping.

### How pregnancy duration and gestational age affect eligibility
The FDA states that mifepristone, when used together with misoprostol, is approved for intrauterine pregnancy through ten weeks gestation (70 days or less since the first day of the last menstrual period) [N2-F2]. That means the pregnancy must be within that window to be medically eligible for home use. The Guttmacher Institute notes that several studies have reported medical abortion up to 9 weeks gestation through telemedicine services as safe and generally well tolerated, but it also emphasizes that legal restrictions may require earlier provider involvement in some states [N3-F3]. The ACOG practice bulletin similarly notes that most patients at 70 days of gestation or less who desire abortion are eligible for a medication abortion, but there are medical conditions for which medication abortion may not be appropriate [N3-R2]. In short, gestational age is not just a numerical limit; it determines whether the regimen is medically appropriate and whether the patient meets the FDA-approved window.

### Which medications are used and how they should be taken
The FDA-approved regimen is 200 mg mifepristone orally on day one, then 800 mcg misoprostol buccally 24 to 48 hours later, with follow-up with a healthcare provider about 7 to 14 days after mifepristone [N2-F2]. Planned Parenthood describes the home steps in more detail: first take mifepristone, then misoprostol 24 to 48 hours later, and for misoprostol, the preferred methods are buccal, sublingual, or vaginal, with specific instructions on how to place the pills and leave them for 30 minutes [N1-F1]. The same source stresses that the pills should not be swallowed, because that may make them less effective and more likely to cause nausea [N1-F1]. So the regimen is not simply “take two pills” but requires precise timing and administration.

### What screening or confirmation is needed before starting
Before starting, provider confirmation is required. The FDA explicitly states that mifepristone should not be used if the pregnancy is more than 70 days since the first day of the last menstrual period, and it lists several contraindications including ectopic pregnancy, adrenal problems, long-term corticosteroid use, bleeding problems, anticoagulant use, inherited porphyria, and an IUD in place [N2-F2]. The Cleveland Clinic adds that medical abortion is contraindicated in patients who are too far along, allergic to the medications, have ectopic pregnancy, or use certain other medications [N4-R4]. The IPAS source adds that mifepristone and misoprostol do not treat ectopic pregnancy and may delay diagnosis and treatment of this life-threatening condition [N2-R3]. In other words, provider confirmation is not optional; it is necessary to establish eligibility and identify any red flags.

### Contraindications and red flags that require stopping
The FDA’s Q&A states that mifepristone is contraindicated in patients with confirmed or suspected ectopic pregnancy, and that it should not be used if the pregnancy is more than 70 days since the first day of the last menstrual period [N2-F2]. The Cleveland Clinic similarly lists ectopic pregnancy and allergy to the medications as contraindications [N4-R4]. The evidence also shows that serious adverse events can occur, including deaths from ectopic pregnancy or sepsis, and that healthcare providers should watch for signs and symptoms in patients who have taken mifepristone [N2-F2]. This means the patient should not proceed if they have any of these red flags, and should instead seek provider assessment immediately.

## 2) Risks and limitations of doing it at home without professional oversight

Home use of medication abortion carries several important risks and limitations. First, complications and incomplete abortion are possible, and follow-up is essential. Planned Parenthood notes that some people will need follow-up treatment to complete the abortion, and that follow-up appointments are important to make sure the abortion is complete and the person is feeling well [N4-R2]. The Cleveland Clinic similarly states that follow-up is recommended within 2 to 5 weeks, and that follow-up appointments may ask the patient to come in for further care [N4-R1]. A second major limitation is that the safety and effectiveness of the regimen depend on precise timing, dosage, and method of administration. The Royal Women’s Hospital similarly stresses that follow-up is important to make sure the abortion is complete and the person is feeling well [N4-R3]. Without that oversight, complications such as incomplete abortion, heavy bleeding, infection, or ectopic pregnancy may go unrecognized until they become urgent.

A fourth limitation is that legal and provider-guided requirements may prevent full self-direction. The Guttmacher Institute explains that many states impose restrictions on medication abortion, such as requiring in-person visits after the regimen, limiting provision to physicians only, or prohibiting mailing abortion pills [N3-F3]. These restrictions exist even when the FDA-approved regimen is medically appropriate, which shows that self-directed care may not be legally available in many jurisdictions. The same source also notes that states may require medically inaccurate information about “reversing” medication abortion, which can confuse patients and undermine informed choice [N3-F3]. This means that even if a person wants to do it at home, they may face legal barriers that require provider involvement.

Finally, self-guided use is limited by the inability to confirm accurate gestational age and pregnancy status. The evidence in this wave does not provide a single, universally definitive home-based pregnancy-dating method, but it does show that accurate dating is important for eligibility and safety. The FDA’s Q&A explicitly ties mifepristone use to gestational duration and states that the regimen is approved for pregnancy through ten weeks gestation [N2-F2]. ## 3) Legal, ethical, and counseling context

It also notes that several states limit medication abortion provision solely to physicians, which contradicts evidence that advanced practice clinicians can safely provide the regimen [N3-F3]. In addition, some states explicitly prohibit telemedicine provision of medication abortion, and others require in-person exams before medications are provided [N3-F3]. The FDA explicitly states that mifepristone should not be used if the pregnancy is more than 70 days since the first day of the last menstrual period, and it lists several contraindications including ectopic pregnancy, adrenal problems, long-term corticosteroid use, bleeding problems, anticoagulant use, inherited porphyria, and an IUD in place [N2-F2].
